svg.aria-label: Bridges. 1, simple timber beam bridge: build an abutment on each bank, of stone masonry or a timber crib filled with stone, bedded deep in firm ground; lay timber beams on top and planks across the beams, with gaps between the planks and railings on both sides; rest the beam ends on stone, do not bury them in earth; doubling the span doubles the bending moment, or makes it 4 times if the load per metre stays the same; a beam set on edge is stronger than one laid flat; two pine beams about 30 cm in diameter side by side, spanning about 5 m, carry a fully loaded handcart with margin to spare; for spans over about 6-8 m add a pier in the middle or use a truss. 2, stone arch bridge: first build heavy abutments, put up timber centring, lay wedge-shaped stones up from both sides at once, set the keystone last, fill the haunches with stone and earth, and remove the centring slowly once the mortar has hardened; the arch pushes outwards to both sides. 3, suspension bridge: anchor both ends of the main cables to the roots of big trees, boulders or deep-buried logs; the sag is about 1/10 of the span; add handrail ropes on both sides and net them together. 4, testing: inspect first, then load-test by piling heavy weights in the middle of the bridge; first an empty cart, then half load, then full load, one cart at a time; do not cross during a flood
svg.title: Bridges: beam, arch and suspension bridges, and testing

g.text: Bridges: beam, arch, suspension, and testing (schematic, not to scale)
① Simple beam bridge: abutment on each bank, timber beams, cross planks
• The longer the span, the thicker the beam:
for the same load, doubling the span doubles
the bending moment in the middle (4 times if
the load per metre stays the same)
• Example: two pine beams about 30 cm across
side by side, spanning about 5 m, carry a fully
loaded handcart with margin to spare (wood rots
and has knots: leave plenty of margin)
• Span over about 6-8 m: add a pier in the
② Stone arch bridge: the arch turns weight into compression to both ends
Keystone: goes in last, locks the arch

⚠ The arch pushes outwards: if the abutments aren't heavy enough, the springings
slide outwards and the whole bridge collapses
⚠ Without experience build only small spans (a few m); never stand under the arch
③ Suspension bridge: cables in tension, anchored at both ends, sagging
• Main cables: two or more thick

• Add handrail ropes on both sides,

✓ It sways when walked on: only a
few people at a time; don't march
replace it if worn or mouldy
④ Testing and using a bridge (new, long unused, or after a flood)
How far does the beam sag?
1. Inspect first: are the abutments scoured out or
tilting? Are the beams cracked or rotten? (Stab with
a knife: if it goes in easily, the wood is rotten)
2. Load-test slowly: pile stones or sandbags heavier
than the planned load in the middle of the bridge;
watch how far the beam sags, listen for creaking,
and check it springs back when unloaded
3. First an empty cart, then half load, then full load
4. One cart or one animal at a time; don't crowd
people and animals onto the bridge
✓ Put up a sign at the bridge stating the load limit
✓ Inspect once a year, and at once after a flood
☠ Don't cross during a flood: piers and abutments may already be scoured
out, which you can't see from the surface; drifting trees can knock the
bridge down. Better to wait for the water to go down
